In the seemingly peaceful city zoo, Stuart's life was brutally ended with a hatchet, and now it's up to Detective Winston to uncover the truth among suspects Xanthe and Lowell.

As Winston left the precinct, his mind was in a swirlwind. Investigating the murder of Stuart gave him a bone-chilling sensation. The images of the crime scene fresh in his mind. But a crime scene found in a zoo? He needed answers.

Entering the coffee shop where Xanthe worked as a barista, Winston could see several customers waiting in line. Apparently, their coffee was popular in town. Xanthe could be seen behind the bar, engaging her clients, before she gracefully hurried over to the espresso machine. In that hurry, she accidentally drops a piece of paper. A customer quickly pointed it out, and Winston intervened to pick it up. 

"That looks like a list of phone numbers," the customer said, peering over Winston's shoulder and noticing the peculiar numbers. "Those aren't usual business or personal contacts. I work in telecommunications, I know."

"Thank you," Xanthe said, acknowledging the mishap, before busying herself again. 

Winston headed to the bar but opted not to order anything. Instead, he scanned the fallen paper. The now identified phone numbers seemed quite out of place.  

The Zoo's visitor logs showed that Stuart was a regular, showing up daily. He made a mental note of that. There was certainly a connection between Stuart and the coffee shop...with the baristas. Stuart was seen being quite friendly with the baristas, including the newcomer, Mary, whom he praised quite often. 

"Was Stuart a regular here?" Winston asked Xanthe.

"Yes," She responded warmly, "he loved our coffee. Always praised Mary's hand.. She's pretty good, new or not. But you know, I was the one who used to make his coffee. Had his special recipe down, I did," She added, pointing towards a different espresso machine designated for complicated orders.

"Oh, that's interesting. You must have a busy schedule," Winston said offhandedly.

"Oh yeah, it includes working weekends too," Xanthe said, giving off a slight chuckle.

As Winston left the coffee shop, he recalled that Stuart's murder happened on a weekend. Winston knew this wasn't a coincidence, there was a complex web of intrigue developing here, leading him deeper into the mystery.

Winston stared at the emails on Stuart's computer screen, reading about the deep financial holes Lowell had dug for his bank’s high profile clients. The source of these emails was unidentified, but they were enough to start a full-scale fraud investigation. It appeared that the businessman had been trading emails with Stuart not too long ago. It wasn't too hard to figure out why Stuart might've been targeted.

He looked over the police report, his cigar glowing in the dim room. It was late afternoon when the banking industry slows its hustle and bustle, that Stuart was found at the zoo. It was also the same time Lowell had a bank meeting at the branch near the zoo, according to the calendar reminder from Lowell's heavily incriminating laptop.

As Winston took a break from the case files, sipped coffee, and thought about his next move, he knew he needed to get over to the lumber yard. The police had found some rather interesting pieces of evidence there. The man behind the desk at Lowell's bank vouched that he was a regular at the nearby lumber yard and had been for years. With an empty shed filled with sawdust and shards of wood at his home, it made sense where most of the firewood at Lowell's house came from.

Shuffling through the paperwork, Winston found a bank withdrawal receipt from Lowell's office. It was the bank near the zoo. The timing was convenient. As were the missing firewood logs from his backyard. The man certainly had spent a lot of time around there, in the late afternoon.

The next stop for Winston would be the café. Sure enough, the receipts and CCTV footage confirmed that Lowell was a regular there as well and was there around the same time Stuart was at the zoo.

The guy at the lumber yard confirmed that Lowell came in pretty frequently, mostly for firewood and sometimes for tools. Most recently, he had come in for a new hatchet, but he mentioned that his old hatchet was missing from his shed. Strange, considering the murder weapon was a hatchet and it just so happened to match the brand that Lowell usually favored.

In his search, Winston found Lowell's laptop at Stuart's apartment. Through Lowell's email exchanges and Stuart's search history, it became clear that Stuart had found evidence of Lowell's illegal banking operations. These were the same operations he had been contacting the unknown source about. And there were the emails from Stuart himself, asking for a substantial dollar figure to keep quiet.

Winston looked at his notes. He had a lot of work ahead of him, but each interview, each piece of evidence, was knitting together the fabric for Stuart's murder. He ordered another coffee and made a list of questions for Lowell. He had an interesting day ahead of him.

In a bustling office, a mundane bottle of bleach becomes a lethal weapon, leading to the chilling murder of Murray; it's up to the sharp-minded Detective Winston to navigate through a web of deceit spun by Chris and Gloria, the enigmatic suspects.

Winston sat down on the edge of the performance stage, his eyes sweeping the room as he took in the heavily trodden dance floor, the scattered props, and miscellaneous personal belongings of the performers. Just on the edge of the stage, among the sparsely placed chairs and costume racks, he noticed a small bottle of bleach. He confirmed with one of the stagehands that it belonged to Gloria, the Choreographer.

He remembered Gloria once mentioning in passing how dangerous bleach could be if ingested. She also was known to often research on various chemicals for special effects in her choreography sets. A bizarre comment to make about bleach, but in her line of work meticulous hygiene was important. The costumes worn by the dancers were often delicate and required careful cleaning. Gloria was known among the troupe for her attention to the sanitation of their attire.

As Winston considered this, a light flicked on in the office upstairs, an indication that Gloria was still there. She often held late practices and rehearsals in the office building. And those rehearsals often ran over time. "A perfectionist," Winston mumbled under his breath.

Murray, the victim, had frequently been in the office late at night. Alone. Even secretive at times. Winston remembered spotting Murray meeting behind the stage with members of a rival dance group. Something didn't feel right and he paid more attention.

Winston recollected a heated quarrel between Gloria and Murray. Gloria was upset that Murray had leaked her proprietary choreography to the rival dance troupe. This discovery was devastating for Gloria. Her unique, innovative work was out in the open, her career was taking a steep plunge.

Winston stood up and glanced around once more before moving toward the office stairs. Notably, the rehearsal space had no security cameras - no direct way to monitor or record any unusual activities.

He found Gloria still hard at work in the office. She looked up and he could see disappointment and frustration etched on her lined face. "Work hard, but don't work yourself into the ground," Winston commented mildly. 

Gloria smiled ruefully, fingers splayed across scattered scripts and documents, "In this line of work, detective, there isn't much of a choice". 

He only nodded in response but inside, Winston felt a swirl of questions rising up. Unseen connections forming and dissipating too quickly to catch. Time to dig a little deeper.

Winston carried a cup of his favorite diner's coffee in his hand as he walked into Murray's office building. From the dusty files sitting on top of a filing cabinet he picked up an incident report dated three years ago. A player had accidentally ingested cleaning fluid during a practice session and had fallen ill. The report confirmed that Chris was the coach at the time of the incident. 

Stepping to the side, Winston made eye contact with the janitor who was tidying up after the police search. "Some mess this, huh?" Winston asked casually. 

The janitor looked up at him, nodding. "Awful thing," he said, "Murray... poisoned in his office like this, during office hours."

Winston nodded, thinking of Chris's coaching duties operating during the same hours. Chris's knowledge of health and wellness was also apparent from the motivational posters in the gym area, an area which happened to include an office for Chris and a cabinet holding various coaching supplies, including cleaning products such as bleach.

Before he left the building, Winston decided to check the lost and found box at the reception. Among the pile of assorted items, a pair of sunglasses caught his eye. They were Chris's, the receptionist confirmed. 

Winston next set out to a nearby park which was a popular spot for office employees and tourists alike. He found an elderly woman sitting on a park bench, who recounted witnessing Chris in the park earlier. The woman, however, had lost sight of him near the water fountain. 

Pulling out his notebook, Winston jotted down the fact that Chris disappeared from sight near the water fountain. He then went on to speak with a local ice cream seller who confirmed seeing Chris heading into a dense, wooded area within the park. 

Heading back to his car, Winston ran into a group of tourists who claimed to have seen Chris earlier. One of them confirmed that they had seen Chris before he disappeared. 

As he drove back to the precinct, Winston digested the day's findings. In addition to his coaching duties, Chris was responsible for equipment and supply maintenance. He usually operated during office hours, was familiar with cleaning products including bleach, and his office was located in the same building as Murray's.

Target case file:

When Mack's life got fatally bleached out on a soccer field, it was up to Detective Winston to sift through the dark clues left by his suspects: Helen and Danielle.

Winston stared at the crime scene in front of him. The soccer field's lush greenery was marred by the gruesome sight of Mack's lifeless body. His bleached face was contorted in an expression of surprise, as though he couldn't believe what had happened.

"Helen, did you clean up post-game?" Winston posed his question with a stern expression. The corner of his mouth upturned as he noticed a potential clue, but didn’t let it reach his eyes.

"Yes, Detective. As I always do," Helen replied, her face drawn with somberness. Winston noted her impeccably clean appearance and gloves, without a trace of mud despite the weather and her outdoor responsibilities.

Helen was the housekeeper here. Mack, having no family, had entrusted her with the keys to the house, as mentioned in his will. Winston flipped through his notes, recalling that not only did Helen work for Mack, but she came to the game early that day and was still there after everyone had left, right around the time Mack was found dead.

Winston delved a little deeper. "I understand that you enjoy camping, Helen...alone?" 

"Yes, it's my chance to unwind, to hike off trails and be amongst nature. Besides, I enjoy the solitude that these trips offer and prefer not to have any company," Helen added, thereby hinting at why she refused to let anyone join her on these outings.

"I see," Winston said. "And water activities, do you engage in any during these camping trips?"

Taken aback, Helen never expected such a question. "Actually, no. I don't fancy spending time near the water, camping is mostly about the solitude for me."

"Hmm, I see." Winston made a show of jotting this down in his notebook, his eyes never leaving Helen's face.

"The people at the house, do they appreciate your work?" Winston posed his question carefully.

"I’ve overheard malicious conversations about me and my work. It feels...almost humiliating, and objectifying. It hurt to know that the people I care for don’t return the sentiment,” Helen admitted, looking away.

The detective carefully observed Helen, making no judgments. As more pieces clicked into place, he thanked Helen and excused her, promising to update her further on the case. Winston prided himself on his professionalism. His job was simply to collect clues for an often unforgiving puzzle.

He couldn't shake the thought of why a housekeeper, like Helen, who strongly avoided mud and water, went camping so frequently, choosing often to go off the beaten trail. Equally intriguing was her insistence on not allowing others to accompany her on these trips. Hence, he moved on to collecting the next piece of the puzzle, all the while, carefully observing every action, every reaction, and every telltale indicator of deception. The game was still afoot, and Winston would leave no stone unturned.

Detective Winston rubbed his temples, staring at the contents strewn from his bulging file. The victim's name was Mack. The young man had been on the cusp of marriage, though rumors swirled that the engagement was nothing more than an elaborate ruse to satisfy the expectations of his parents.

Winston sighed deeply and continued to scan the case file. There was something unusual about this crime. The murder weapon of choice, a bottle of bleach, was anything but typical, and the name Danielle, scribbled repeatedly throughout his notes, gave the detective pause.

Danielle - a local spiritual guru known throughout the community for her meticulous cleaning. Winston found it curious that someone who used cleanliness as a tool to attain spirituality would find herself mixed up in this grisly case. 

From what the detective had gathered, Danielle had been conducting one of her renowned spiritual sessions the day Mack was killed and with a chilling thought, Winston remembered that Mack could have been one of the attendees. After all, the soccer field where the young man's life was snuffed out was also Danielle's usual haunt for leading her sessions. In fact, she had the whole city at her fingertips, but she always chose the ever-bustling soccer field - a fact he couldn’t dismiss lightly.

Danielle was a fervent believer in spiritual purity and she saw Mack's loveless marriage as a direct threat to that purity. That much was clear to Winston from copious notes and conversations he uncovered. He recalled one particular conversation recorded between Danielle and a friend where, talking about Mack, she had stated fervently, "He needs to remain single. Marriage without love would be catastrophic to his spiritual purity". 

Church conversations known city-wide revealed Mack was ready to be shackled in a loveless marriage, a reality the entire city was privy to. This caught Winston's attention. He was certain Danielle was aware of Mack's arrangement, and it was playing into her concept of purity. This notion was definitely worth exploring.

The curious case of Danielle continued as Winston flicked through the file. Her obsessive cleaning ticked another in a list of oddities surrounding this spiritual guru. Bleach was her go-to choice, and she dedicated her spare time to scrubbing every surface she could reach, her way of achieving external and internal purity - or so she claimed. 

Winston shook his head as he closed the case file, a heavy sigh spewing from his lips. He had more questions now than when he'd started. Danielle’s belief system, her ubiquitous presence at the soccer field, Mack's loveless marriage, and Danielle's passion for cleaning - they all lay like jigsaw puzzle pieces yearning to be fit together. But how? The question remained unanswered as he rose from his seat, his thoughts lost in the intricate web of the case that lay before him.

In an adrenaline inducing bungee jumping site, Mack's thrill-seeking adventure came to a gruesome end by a nunchaku; now, it's up to Detective Winston to unravel the deadly secrets between Mackenzie and Ana.

Winston sat quietly in an unmarked Ford, parked a block away from Mackenzie's downtown apartment building. He observed Mackenzie through his binoculars, watching closely as they hastily unlocked their front door. It had been a long day at the office for Mackenzie and, like clockwork, they were seen taking their customary break on a public bench, working on their laptop.

Before long, Mackenzie was seen through the partially closed blinds of their apartment, sitting at their desk with their laptop open. They had just returned from a local cyber security meetup, a reality Winston discovered after following Mackenzie to the event later that evening. As Winston watched, they shifted their body and their eyes darted around, Winston duly noted on Mackenzie's apparent concern for online privacy.

"Interesting," Winston thought, while making a mental note to do some research on further cyber security meetups occurring in the vicinity.

The next morning, Winston watched Mackenzie walk out of a martial arts training center. As Mackenzie stopped to say goodbye to their instructor, Winston quickly snapped a photo on his phone. In the picture, Winston could clearly see Mackenzie practicing techniques with the unmistakable form of Mackenzie's sturdy nunchaku resting in the backdrop. This gave Winston a clue that his martial arts training includes nunchaku techniques.

Winston's interest peaked further when he followed Mackenzie to a local shop where they were seen purchasing a new set of nunchaku. Even more intriguing was when they examined a pair of cufflinks on display with a yearning look, cufflinks Winston knew were identical to a pair Mack frequently flaunted around. It appeared Mack had things that Mackenzie also desired.

The investigator decided it was time to pay Mackenzie a visit. He knocked on the apartment door and Mackenzie cautiously invited him in.

Pleasantries were briefly exchanged before Winston's gaze quickly fell on the laptop that was resting by some papers next to an open window.

"You always take this with you to work?" Winston inquired, pointing at the laptop.

"Every day," Mackenzie replied, "I can't leave my work at the office."

"Work goes that well, huh?" Winston probed further. "I hear you were recently ... overlooked for a promotion."

At these words, Mackenzie's expression darkened. "I was the top candidate, you know. It should've been mine. Mack, the new guy, he is nothing compared to me, but he takes it. That promotion, the respect I had. Even those cufflinks I have always wanted, somehow Mack always gets to have them."

Winston nodded, making a mental note of Mackenzie's reaction. They turned the conversation to martial arts and during the chat, Mackenzie unintentionally revealed their prowess with nunchaku.

In a small, hidden compartment in Mackenzie's wardrobe, Winston found the pair of nunchaku that Mackenzie had recently purchased. He swiftly snapped a picture of this evidence before closing the wardrobe.

As the day grew late, Winston thanked Mackenzie for their time and headed out, feeling more certain than ever about the path his investigation was following.

Winston sat in his office, photos of Mack --the bungee jumper found dead-- scattered heartbreakingly across his desk. The lack of clues at the murder site puzzled him, nothing seemed out of place. All he had was an unusual weapon, the nunchaku, not something he’d found at too many crime scenes.

Standing up, he straightened his tie and headed to the shared housing complex of the victim and suspect. Ana Diaz lived here, along with Mack. Ground rules for questioning the suspect were laid out in his mind.

Ana received him with a stoic expression and invited him inside. Her suitcase was unpacked, strewn helter-skelter around the room. She explained she had come back from the bungee jumping site late last night, still in shock about Mack’s murder.

Nunchaku lay on the table. Winston noticed, she explained it as the normal household item of a martial artist. She said she practices martial arts at the same bungee jumping location. 

Asked about their shared occupation, she sighed heavily. “Mack loved it, though," She said, "He was the instigator, insisting everyone take the jump.”

Ana seemed to soften, talking about her faith, her traditions. “Bungee jumping, it's against my beliefs,” she admitted, “but I’d signed up too, expecting some ridicule like always.”

Ridicule. That was a word Winston had already heard before concerning Mack. He asked around, among their friends, everyone said the same, Mack liked to joke, to point fun at beliefs. Especially Ana’s it seemed.

They left together, Ana and Mack, the morning of the murder, people had seen them. Winston asked why, given their strained relationship. Ana shrugged off, her hands trembling. “He wasn’t too bad,” she replied. 

Nobody else was documented at the bungee jumping site that day, only Mack and Ana. It was time to head there. Winston thanked Ana for her time and left, driving straight to the scene. He stared up at the looming diving board, picturing the scene.  

Only two people there that day, Mack and Ana. He looked around, the martial arts practice ground nearby held the last piece. Nunchaku, a common weapon in martial arts practices. He tested one, the weight fitting neatly into his palm while he surveyed the area. This was the scene he needed to piece together.

In the tranquil sphere of the temple, Charlotte's demise by barbed wire disrupts the serenity, drawing Detective Winston into a puzzling web woven by suspects Priscilla and Xenia.


Winston unfolded the clipped newspaper announcement of Charlotte's upcoming wedding. He scanned the quaint details, turning each over in his mind. The setting was a temple, a peculiar choice within their community. Unique also, was the choice of Xenia as the wedding planner. A woman known for her fastidiousness and deft hands in crafting seamless events. 

In a recent chat with Charlotte before her wedding, she mentioned a peculiar detail regarding a certain secret she was advised by Xenia to keep hidden - her past relationship with Xenia's current partner. It was a secret she was planning to unveil at the altar, a revelation that would surely raise a few eyebrows, with Xenia no longer being the lone keeper of it.

"Ms. Xenia, I presume?" Winston asked, entering the wedding planner's office. 

"Yes. How can I aid you detective?" Xenia responded, with a slight surprise in her eyes.

"I wanted to talk about Charlotte's wedding... a ceremony that was slated to occur at the exact minute of her murder. Noticed anything unusual around those days?” Winston queried.

Xenia hesitated, her expression wavering. It was clear that the jab about Charlotte's intention to confess the past, which involved Xenia's significant other, had struck a nerve. The anger simmering in Xenia's eyes was volatile and intense, enough to make anyone uncomfortable.

As they conversed, Winston's attention drifted to an office closet, slightly ajar. A suitcase peeked from within, stuffed with neatly folded clothes, almost as though it was constantly ready for a trip. His colleagues had often mentioned seeing this suitcase during their routine meetings with Xenia.

"Ever much of a traveler, Xenia?" Winston asked casually. 

She seemed taken aback by his question. "Sometimes... it's part of the job. Last minute trips for a desired decoration, or perhaps to get a gift. Weekend trips and all."

"That your suitcase in the closet, always packed and ready?" Winston nodded towards it. Xenia followed his gaze toward the suitcase, then back at him. "Yes, why?" 

"No reason," Winston shrugged. "It’s just that colleagues have mentioned spotting you with your luggage at the airport, and at the train station buying tickets – during work hours."

"Yeah, like I said, travelling becomes part of the job sometimes,” countered Xenia, smoothly.

Throughout their conversation about wedding preparations, Xenia specified that she was responsible for every minute detail – setting up and breaking down the décor, liaising with the temple people, overseeing every aspect of the event. She emphasized that her duties required her presence before, during, and after the ceremony. Winston mentally jotted this down, noticing how neatly these timings coincided with those of Charlotte's unfortunate fate.

Winston rose to depart, conveying his gratitude, "Thanks for your time."

"Of course, anything to help," Xenia replied softly. “Charlotte's passing is shocking, but remember, we rely on trust and reputation in our business. It's all we have. Charlotte's confession could have marred that."

Detective Winston sifted through the papers littering his desk. Crime scene photos mixed with witness statements and information on both the victim, Charlotte, and the potential suspect, Priscilla. Winston ran a hand through his hair, taking a deep breath.

Eyewitness accounts placed Priscilla at the temple on the day of the crime. The same temple where Charlotte was found, her life taken by barbed wire. Winston's gaze drifted towards some photos of the hiking trails Priscilla was known to frequent. The trails, all too often, wound their way past the same temple where Charlotte met her end.

Pushing the papers around, Winston found a report from the local police. Priscilla's involvement with certain gang activities was far from a well-kept secret. The faded gang tattoos on Priscilla's skin were testament to her affiliation. Charlotte, on the other hand, was part of a rival gang, a fact anyone could see from the tags she left behind. 

Photos from the trails Priscilla often hiked showed a significant amount of barbed wire fencing. Winston mused, barbed wire was indeed common along these trails - so much so that Priscilla had even learned to utilize items like it in her own survival knowledge on these hiking expeditions. 

A picture of Priscilla hiking caught Winston's attention. He noted the pair of wire snips she carried. Those would be potentially useful in dealing with the surplus of barbed wire on her usual trails. He also noted the rough timeline on the police report. Charlotte's time of death matched up too neatly with the time witnesses had spotted Priscilla at the temple that day.

"Interesting, isn't it?" Winston muttered to himself, mulling over the facts at hand. Pushing his chair back, he decided it was time to ask Priscilla some questions. He was determined to learn the truth, one piece of evidence at a time.

In the glimmering lights and pulsating bass of the local roller rink, Wendy met her brutal end with a pickaxe, leaving Detective Winston the unenviable task of untangling suspect stories from Marianne and Sidney.

Detective Winston tapped his pen against the mugshot of Marianne. She wore the hardened expression of a seasoned miner, and a sprinkle of white dust beaded her forehead. She had, years ago, spent a considerable amount of time underground before she traded the pickaxe for a ring. Even after her marriage, however, Winston knew that Marianne was not unfamiliar with the heft and purpose of such a tool.

His eyes consisted of the audit papers laid out before him, declaring a significant debt that Marianne owed in back taxes. She was circling financial demise, and the state was closing in. Then, his eyes shifted to the statement provided by a friend of hers, highlighting her strong assertion that she would rather perish than get sent behind bars. It seemed to Winston that Marianne was still filled with the spirits of the old miners, willing to risk it all in pursuit of her own freedom.

His venture out to her parcel of land a few days back had stamped the image in his mind of her mining tools lounging out in the open. They were well-kept and clean, the way old miners kept their tools. Marianne had been spotted around the community with the pickaxe, using it for various garden works and general maintenance.

Now Winston's attention moved to Wendy, the victim, an honest lady known for her earnest ways. She was found in a sequestered section of the roller rink, a roller skate still hanging onto her foot as if she was frozen mid-skate.

Placing a call, Winston requested the CCTV footage of the roller rink from the night of the murder. There, in the flickering low resolution, was Wendy locked in a heated argument with Marianne. The dispute ended and Wendy skated off, but Marianne stayed.

Later, another clip showed Marianne lingering along the outskirts, long after the other skaters had left. It was an eerie sight - the roller rink was empty, except for the flickering neon lights and Marianne, circling the rink with an unsettling calmness.

Winston slid an envelope towards himself and carefully extracted a photograph. It was Wendy's last piece of brave detective work - a picture of Marianne caught in a grim action that served as undeniable proof of her crime. But it was Wendy, with her unwavering integrity, who held this tight to her chest, vowing to expose the truth about Marianne.

Two cups of coffee empty, Winston switched off the lights and left the room. The image of Marianne and the pickaxe lingered in the darkness of the office, the unsaid words and whispers of the CCTV footage bouncing off the walls. The unwelcome truth seemed to have found a perfect partner with the impending dawn, unflinching and relentless.

As Winston flipped through the case file, his eyes landed on a photo of the crime scene. His heart ached slightly for the young woman, Wendy, brutally murdered at the roller rink. The weapon of choice: a pickaxe. Not something you would typically see at a roller rink.

Entering the rink, Winston felt a shudder creep up his spine as he glanced at the spot where Wendy's body had been found. Shaking off his unease, he made his way over to the row of lockers where the staff pointed him to Sidney's locker.

It was well known that Sidney, a local geologist, was a regular at this establishment. Even given the oddity of a geologist frequenting a roller rink, Winston was familiar enough with murder investigations to understand that people, like rocks, had layers. 

Casually, Winston made conversation, "You're here a lot, I hear?" Sidney nodded, almost dismissively, not yet prepared to show his hand. "I heard you often chat about your friend Jack, is that right?" Sidney nodded again, this time more cautiously.

"I find skating to be a wonderful escapism," Sidney murmured, while scanning the rink with a haunted look. His guard dropped slightly as he added, "And Jack...well, you know about Jack and his troubles."

From an interrogation room in the local precinct, Jack, a known criminal and Sidney's friend, gazed at Winston. Already serving time, he had nothing to lose by divulging information. As Sidney’s name left Winston's lips, Jack's eyes grew wide.

"He's a letter writer, you know. Always has been," Jack offered, unprompted. Winston thought curiously about the possible relevance of this. Jack continued, now with a dropped voice, "He cherishes the art of placing words on paper."

Caught off guard by the reverence in Jack's words, Winston's attention piqued at the news that Sidney was a common pen pal.

At the roller rink office, Sidney's tormented expression flitted across the screen of the surveillance camera footage. There he was with Wendy, both laughing and skating. The timestamp below the image – the night of Wendy’s death. As the staff had mentioned, Sidney’s presence during the hours coinciding with the murder fit. There was little doubt that he had been in the vicinity.

Winston packed his notepad away and left for Sidney's apartment. There, the detective found an abundance of stamps and stationary stacked neatly by the desk. A typewriter nearby indicated an air of old-school character. Jack's words suddenly resurfaced. Scanning the room again, Winston spotted a picture of Wendy. Beside it, a letter with Sidney's handwriting.

Hands in his slick black overcoat pockets, Winston glanced around the roller rink one last time before leaving. Stopping at the doorway, he turned around to Sidney, opening his mouth to say something before deciding against it. Winston remembered their previous conversation. "I have no idea what Wendy was talking about," Sidney had said defiantly when confronted with the secret Wendy had been spreading about him.

Suddenly, Winston remembered what he had heard in side conversations with Wendy's friends. The secret she knew wasn't just ruinous; it was humiliating. She knew something that, once revealed, would publicly disgrace Sidney. 
                    
With a sigh, he discarded the thought and walked out into the chill of the evening. His mind buzzed with unanswered questions. There was more to this case. More to Sidney. More to Wendy. To think it all revolved around a roller rink. He'll crack it open, he always does.

In the dim light of an abandoned factory, Kaylee's lifeless body lay with the cold steel of a pickaxe lodged within, thrusting Detective Winston into a dark game of deception with suspects Penelope and Francis.

Winston breathed a sigh of relief as he entered the comfort of his car, escaping the oppressive heat outside. The day had been anything but a usual one and he reviewed the paper on his clipboard yet again. Kaylee, a young woman, was found dead in an abandoned factory of all places and the purported weapon was a pickaxe, an old miner's pickaxe to be exact.

His next interview was scheduled with a nanny named Penelope. Penelope was not your average nanny. Alongside her formal education in early child care, she also had professional training in the same field, acquiring skills that allowed her to excel in handling children. Despite her credible qualifications, Winston found it decidedly strange to connect a nanny with such a gruesome find, not least because Penelope herself had most of her busy day spent with children, not in an old factory.

After a short walk, he approached a modest suburban home quite close to the abandoned factory. The home itself, despite its proximity, seemed worlds apart from the grim discovery location. 

Penelope greeted him at the door, shaking his hand with a warm smile. "Hello, Penelope." Winston greeted, then a thought hit him. A person of her profession is typically responsible for a child's growth and upbringing. Penelope's studied and trained background in childcare had indeed stuck in his mind since their last encounter.

During their conversation, Winston learned that Penelope was seen leaving her house around the estimated time of the murder. Interestingly enough, he even had a witness claiming to see Penelope with an old mining pickaxe earlier that day, a claim solidly backed up as the recovered pickaxe, the very same weapon used in the murder, matched exactly the one described by the witness.

Just as he was thinking about the pickaxe, a piece of evidence from the crime scene flashed across his mind. Winston reached into his jacket pocket to pull out a page from a diary. It was from Kaylee's diary. The entry was clear; Kaylee had a meeting scheduled with Penelope at the so-called abandoned factory.

A unease washed over Winston, making the usually delicious coffee taste sour in his mouth. Kaylee seemed to have known something about Penelope that she didn't want public. She had unearthed something about Penelope's past... maybe even criminal past. The parents didn't know... and Kaylee was planning to tell.

He glanced at Penelope, who was sitting across from him, looking anxious. She must've known that the exposure would cause her serious embarrassment... and at worst, cost her her job. With no other events reported that could have prevented Kaylee from meeting Penelope, it all looped back to the meeting at the factory.

"Well, Penelope, I do have a long walk back to my car." he said, finishing the last of his coffee and standing up. "I've taken enough of your time, thank you for your cooperation." He gave a nod as he reached the door, leaving the nanny to contemplate her day filled with children, and his with unanswered questions.

Detective Winston grimaced, finally setting down the carefully documented police case file of the late Kaylee. The coffee stains on the file folder began to bleed into the corners of the cover. The pangs of guilt for indulging in too much work in the form of an overbrewed cup of joe were not his only concern. An image haunted him; it was from a video footage where Francis had caught Kaylee red-handed, threatening his daughter which he digitally recorded as proof.

Shaking the sudden chill from his spine, Winston looked out of his office window to the abandoned factory where Kaylee had been found. Francis, Kaylee's husband, had years of mining experience and was renowned for his pickaxe expertise. Francis had arranged the meeting point and was seen coaxing her into trusting that the factory would be undisturbed.

The town had all been abuzz with this unthinkable murder. Kaylee's constant torment of Francis' daughter, enough to induce anxiety and depression in the child, was now common knowledge. Even more upsetting was the unusual delicateness Francis had shown in handling this situation, a man known for his work involving grueling physical labor that required a high level of strength and endurance.

Digging into his pocket Winston pulled out the receipt for the pickaxe that he'd found in Francis’ pocket, a peculiar coincidence considering Francis’ mining background and the tool associated with it.

In the corner of his foul-smelling, second-hand leather bound desk was a photograph. A crisp, clear frame showing Francis purchasing the said pickaxe at the local hardware store. It was not surprising that Francis had chosen to arm himself with a tool he was already so familiar with, but to invite his wife into a murderous trap of his creation was another level of distressing reality.

Winston looked up to see Francis standing in the doorway, tall and solemn. "Detective Winston," he said quietly, "We need to talk about Kaylee."

Winston nodded, gesturing for him to take a seat. "I heard about what happened. About the threats she made to your daughter."

Francis looked taken aback, his gaze shifting around the room. "Yes...I caught her threatening our daughter. I don't know why she couldn't see what her actions were doing to our daughter."

Winston nodded but said nothing. He stayed silent, letting Francis explain in his own time, about the factory meeting he'd arranged with Kaylee, his knowledge that the factory would have been empty at that time, the purchased pickaxe and the chilling threats Kaylee had aimed towards his daughter.

As Francis left his office, Winston glanced back at the file, picking up the coffee cup, he pondered the gritty mysteries life tended to serve up.

In the heart of a verdant rainforest, Isla had tragically met her end by a lead pipe, prompting Detective Winston to start sifting through the eerie silence, with Jesse and Brian as the prime suspects.

Winston frowned in concentration while browsing through the piles of family photos placed tastefully on a side table at the ceremony.  Isla, the beautiful young woman, was the star in almost every picture. Winston scanned every photo meticulously, but Brian, who had been a janitor for the family for many years, was nowhere to be found.

His attention was diverted from the photographs when the back door of the mortuary creaked open, and Brian stepped in hesitantly. He seemed self-conscious about his tardiness, his back hunched and his gaze darting around the room. Winston glanced over at the service in progress. Brian wasn’t mentioned as a friend or a relative during the service, but he stayed until the end of the burial, lingering as the crowd started to disperse. His aloof demeanor piqued Winston’s interest.

The next day found Winston scanning the tools in Brian's workspace. As per his janitorial duties, Brian handled an assortment of tools, the most common of which were lead pipes. His workspace deep in the jungle revealed that he had been working there for many years, in fact, over a decade, blending his job with nature, dirt, and rust.

Winston remembered that a witness had seen Brian cleaning in the rainforest, a lead pipe in hand, on the same day Isla’s body was discovered. Brian was probably mending a burst pipe he had mentioned to Winston during a casual conversation. The rainforest, where Isla had been brutally murdered, was - oddly enough - a second home to Brian. Rainforest cleaning sounded strange to Winston but perhaps that was the way of life here.

The rainforest echoed with the sounds of both man-made and natural life around him. Winston watched the intricate work Brian was involved in. As the detective, he mused, "So, I hear you've been here a while," while eyeing Brian maneuver a lead pipe he was using to fix a water valve.

"Yep, over a decade now," was Brian's gruff reply, his hands occupied. He paused to wipe his brow with a grimy arm. "It's quite peaceful here, you know."

Winston's gaze lingered on Brian before he divulged, "You were spotted here around the same time Isla was murdered." Their eyes met for a moment before Winston disappeared back into the foliage.

Detective Winston leaned against his cruiser, his eyes tracking the locals as they went about their daily lives. Faces lit up and heads turned as the rhythmic sound of drumming floated through the air. The source of this daily ritual was Jesse, a powerhouse drummer whose status in the town was akin to that of a local hero—a status enjoyed due to his immense talent on the drums.

Winston watched Jesse for a moment longer, taking in the muscles that rippled in his arms as he played. His talent was undeniable, his every beat pounding out a rhythm that seemed to embody the heart of the community itself. He had spent countless hours practicing, strengthening his upper body and arms through his ceaseless devotion to drumming.

Breaking away from the crowd, Winston took the path that led through the rainforest. Evidence suggested that Jesse visited this place often—where he drew inspiration from the symphony of nature itself and penned down melodies. It was known that his best works as a drummer were composed here. Wandering deeper into the rainforest, Winston couldn't help but try to see this place as Jesse might.

A few days ago, Jesse had overheard Isla's nervous whispers about her intent to confess something incriminating to the police, something concerning Jesse himself. The knowledge threw him into a state of unease. Fearing what Isla might reveal about his involvement in illegal activities—activities she had discovered herself—had let the rhythm of Jesse's drumming take a harsher beat. 

An association with a metalworking shop came up during the preliminary investigation.  This was the place where Jesse had learned to customize his drumsticks himself, favoring lead piping instead of the usual. It was a small token of uniqueness he added to his music but somehow felt out of sync with the rest.

Returning to his cruiser, Winston pulled out a notepad, flipping to a blank page. Isla's name was written at the top, her connection to Jesse much more than casual. In her possession were the evidence of Jesse's illegal activities capable of damaging, if not entirely ruining Jesse's career and standing in the community.

The pounding of the drums echoed through the stillness of the rainforest, lending an ominous tone to the otherwise peaceful atmosphere. Jesse was aware of his imminent predicament—an inevitable reckoning with his secrets, aided by Isla's confessions.

Another day in the town ended, and with it, Jesse's drumming ceased. But for him, his day was far from over. His routine entailed hours of practice and composing, maintaining his superiority in the art. Jesse's skill was a result of his consistent hard work and dedication, his muscular prowess a testament to both.

For Detective Winston, Jesse was a suspect, committing a crime possibly to protect a secret shrouded by the rhythm of his drums. As he drove away, the murmuring of the locals filled his ears, talking excitedly about Jesse's session for the day. A crime in the community, a rhythm disrupted. The chapter that unfolded was far from melodious.

In the middle of pliés and pirouettes, a deadly crossbow bolt finds its mark, leaving Ryan lifeless in the dance studio and launching Detective Winston into a tense pas de deux with suspects Rex and Mandy.

Detective Winston had barely finished his coffee when he received the call about the murder at the dance studio. Ryan, a notable figure and beloved dance instructor and advocate for racial integration, was found dead in the wee hours of the morning. The news from the officer stated that there was only one person present, Rex, at the time of the murder. 

Crossbow, a peculiar choice of weapon, but Rex was a known historical weapons enthusiast and was found alone in the studio. Rex was a man known in the community to frequently utter his disgust and hatred for other races. He never shied away from making his views known and didn't even care about the public backlash he received.

Winston quickly drove to the scene. His previous encounters with Rex had taught him that he was not the type to embrace change. Rex was a man of his unpleasant prejudices and it's appalling how such hatred could run so deep.

Walking into the studio's vast echoing space, Winston noticed Rex hunched over a droning gramophone, a scattering of musical notes scattered on the floor. As if revealing a questionable love affair, the air was robust with the scent of violin rosin and vintage tunes. It was evident that Rex had been working that night on his compositions.

Rex then stated, in his usual gruff manner, "Found something?" 

"I guess hard work pays off in its own way," Rex replied, confirming his solitary presence during the late work hours coinciding with Ryan's death.

"What an extravagant collection!" Winston commented, looking at the decorated wall filled with a series of historical crossbows that Rex had acquired from an auction. Winston remembered people mentioning how Rex often admired his collection and how he even took crossbow-shooting classes. He noted the empty space in the wall display.

“Yeah, I even took crossbow-shooting classes. Fascinating history behind each of them…” Rex trailed off, a twisted smile on his face. 

Against the backdrop of Rex's repeated disapproval of Ryan's integration views, the altercations Rex had with people from different races, and his significant collection of ancient weapons, Winston made it a point to investigate deeper into Rex's background and his activities during the late-night hours of composing music.

Winston took a sip of coffee and set down the crime scene photos. Laying there was Ryan, a well-known political figure who had been involved in numerous scandals. His reputation was on thin ice, and his sudden death was making waves.

The unexpected detail in this case was the murder weapon, an uncommon choice - a crossbow. Word on the street, and confirmed by Mandy’s friends as they testified at the precinct, was that Mandy, a local tour guide, had an intimate relationship with the departed. Mandy had confided in them, and their testimonies, along with photos of Mandy and Ryan in intimate situations, could back this up. Unconfirmed, but still a lead nonetheless.

Winston had done a little homework on the suspects and had found out that Mandy was not only into medieval war tactics and frequented the local archery range, practicing with the specific type of crossbow the murder was committed with. This alluring detail landed her on the suspect list.

Winston finished his coffee, grabbed his coat, and headed out to meet Mandy. His briefcase also enclosed evidence of her fingerprints taken from the identical crossbow he found in her vast collection during a quick search warrant operation prior.

The sun shone brightly on Mandy as she stood at the entrance to the local museum, her usual station. 

"Hi there, are you Mandy?" Winston asked after her tour group had depart.

"Taking an interest in the local sights, detective?" she replied with a smirk. "Let's just focus on the tour," she tried to redirect, clearly uncomfortable with the topic. 

"Mandy, we need to chat. About Ryan," he narrowed his gaze slightly. "I was hoping we could talk here, if you don't mind."

Mandy's features tensed up a bit; she looked away from Winston and started pointing out a nearby sculpture. "We don't need to bring up the past, let's instead admire the beauty of the Roman Centurion standing tall there," she said, once again trying to steer the conversation.

"No, I'm sorry, it's just that–" 

A sudden wailing siren interrupted their conversation.

"Wait here, please," Winston asked before taking the call. 

When Winston returned after a minute, Mandy had a look of discomfort that strained the corners of her eyes, but she quickly tried to hide it behind a smile. "Talking about the past can be… difficult."

"I've heard you were critically involved in the election campaign." Winston mentioned carefully, causing Mandy to look subtly relieved. 

A hit and a miss. He was on the right track. Picking up the photos taken from Mandy's home, he found what he needed. Mandy had her secrets and he had a job to do. 

Returning to his car, Winston spelled a silent thanks for the fresh pile of leads waiting for him back at the station, still lost in thought about the case.

In the picturesque world of paragliding, hidden secrets tumble as Detective Winston investigates the brutal hatchet murder of Travis, with only Bryan and Everett in the center of the storm.

Rubbing the backside of his eyes, Winston slowly navigated the case photos scattered across his desk. A paragliding site, bloody and as wide open as the sea, was the setting for Travis's murder. Bryan, known more for his cooking than as a suspect, stepped into the limelight of Winston's investigation. 

It did not go unnoticed that Bryan would carry a hatchet on him for his job; the tool in hand was a common sight that everyone had become accustomed to. Par for the course, it was largely ignored when Bryan was seen sharpening his utensil before the incident; a hatchet taught to kiss the air during Bryan's past hatchet throwing competitions. 

Travis was a known occurence on the local gliding scene. Bryan was his assistant, charged with food and drinks, presumably there to manage as the paragliders soared high above.

"So, you're always left to care for the gliders' needs during the flights, huh?" Winston asked, making sure to keep his tone casual as they approached Bryan, who was preparing a meal.

"Yeah, been doing it for a while now. Help 'em grab a bite at the end of their flight, you know?" Bryan mentioned, chopping some tough ingredients with his hatchet. From his posture and technique, it was clear he knew his way around such a tool.

"The same way you've been helping yourself to the petty cash, I see," Winston casually remarked, causing Bryan to stumble a bit, resulting in him nicking his finger slightly.

"No, that's not..." Bryan lapsed before continuing, his hands trembling. He seemed to be genuinely frightened of the possibility of going to jail.

"Travis didn't seem to think so," Winston subtly pointed out, before changing the topic. "How'd you feel about his pranks?"

Bryan's grip on his hatchet tightened, "He's... been a real handful. Those weren’t just pranks, he's been doing everything in his power to make a fool out of me."

"I suppose you were near the gliding site before the incident happened?" Bryan nodded, confirming that he indeed was, "Yeah, I was there prepping up the food and drinks we're serving today."

In the pink-tinged evening light, Winston walked back from the crime scene towards his car. Whispers of unfriendly pranks, public humiliation, and petty thefts filled the air. Across his mind slipped an image of Travis, alone, soaring in the air.

Detective Winston sat back in his chair, brows furrowed as he perused the pile of evidence on the sturdy wooden table. He meticulously studied the hapless victim - Travis, a man recently celebrated for his acrobatic skills on a paraglider, a man whose life was cut short at a paragliding site with a hatchet.

His suspect was intriguing, to say the least. Everett he was known as, a bright-faced man whose talent lay in the realm of woodworking methods. Interestingly, a majority of his time was dedicated to curating displays of impeccable craftsmanship at the local woodworking museum.

Upon arriving at the museum, Winston took a mental note of the serene aura surrounding Everett. His hands, worn from years of delicate crafting, fondly caressed the various tools in his personal collection. Quiet admiration sparked in his eyes as he studied each piece. The hatchet, which was the murder weapon, had been sourced from this same collection.

Everett had a dubious past, considering he had been privy to the office that housed a drawer filled with FFID cards, each bearing a different alias. The coincidental catalog of names was a matching list to Everett's known aliases.

In a room full of bustling conference attendees, Fraser, a local woodworker, casually recollected an incident about an 'Edward' who introduced himself during a conversation at a conference. This character sketch fit Everett impeccably. Yet another time, Winston learned, Everett introduced himself as 'Eric' within a gathering of familiar faces.

His evenly-toned voice was lit with envy as he recalled the numerous paragliding events where he would always find himself under the grand shadow of the deceased Travis. This bitterness was further accentuated by a recent event where Travis triumphed over Everett for a highly acclaimed paragliding award.

"Do you do much woodworking yourself?" Winston asked.

Everett's eyes softened, his hands gripped tighter around the intricate carving in his hand. "Yes, indeed," he replied. "It's the one thing that brings me peace..."

Parallel to the photo of Travis, paragliding expert propelled to international fame, an unsigned artisan found solace in chipping away at blocks of wood, longing for the same acclaim.

In the dense, dank heart of the rainforest, Skylar's life was brutally silenced with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a labyrinth of lies, offered up by the two prime suspects - Albert and Mya.

Winston entered the bustling atmosphere of a large family gathering, all clatter and congratulations on a reunion well-needed. His gaze shifted to a tall woman energetically engaging with her relatives, her vibrant energy palpable amongst the crowd. That would be Mya, the adventurous cousin of the unfortunate victim, Skylar.

He noticed the polished locket adorning her neck, catching the light beautifully, but a sombre contrast to its owner's lively charm.

Exuding friendly charm, Winston approached her, "Mya, may I have a couple of moments?"

"Of course, detective. How may I help you?"

"I understand you and Skylar used to explore your adventurous side together," Winston mentioned casually, trying not to stir any emotional discomfort.

Mya's face softened, "Yes. We both shared a love for the wilderness. Just last week, she invited me on a camping trip to the rainforest. It was harmonious escapades until…” she trailed off.

“Aye, I’m sorry for your loss, Mya.”  
 
Winston noticed the emphasis on her well-toned physique - a strong and agile body, built on a rigorous exercise routine and several hiking and mountain climbing expeditions successfully completed over the years.

Later on, Winston got an opportunity to evaluate the surveillance video of the day Skylar went missing. A quiet scene it was, with only a single instance of incoming and no outgoing traffic - a four-wheel-drive carrying two adventurous souls - Skylar and Mya - into the depths of the rainforest.

Winston’s keen eyes caught the glimpse of Mya’s camping gear. It sure was well stocked - ropes, food supplies, a lead pipe, tents, boots… A lead pipe. The very same, that had turned brutal enough to end a life in the tranquil rainforest.

At Mya’s, while she was away, Winston could only find her camping gear partially scattered in disarray. The lead pipe was blatantly missing.

In a cruiser parked down the street, Winston watched Mya jog up to the deadly rainforest, maybe a run to process her grief, or maybe it was part of her regular exercise routine. Winston watched Mya stoop suddenly and pick something up. A glint of gold. Later, at the reunion, the piece was identified as Skylar’s locket around Mya’s neck. A locket that mysteriously went missing after Skylar's demise and never returned to the rightful inheritors.

Winston took a deep breath. There was so much more to untangle in the mysterious disappearance of Skylar. The case continued to thicken, deeper into the rainforest.

Casual drizzle splattered against the umbrella of Winston as he stood by the yellow cab, its windows slick with rain and partially hiding the figure inside. He knocked twice against the window before it hesitantly slid down, revealing the rough and worn face of Albert, a cab driver who had been working these city streets for longer than most would care to remember. 

"Albert," Winston began, pulling out his badge to cut off any question of his identity. "Seems like you're having a quiet night."

"Just like every other night in this forsaken city," Albert responded bitterly, his hands, the hands of a man used to hard labor, tightening around the taxi steering wheel. 

"I heard about your baseball career back in college. Must have been exciting times," Winston remarked, casually glancing at a lead pipe secured beneath the driver's seat. "Got to make sure feelings of nostalgia don't lead to some baseball practice, especially not in a city like ours."

Albert hesitated for a moment, before answering, "It's for safety. Different times…"

Winston nodded, turning towards the rainforest in the distance. Albert followed his gaze, "Crazy what happened. I was just driving her, Skylar...that is, to the rainforest. The city loved her, I've even seen people switch cabs to ride with her."

"Must have been a challenge," Winston said, subtly hinting at the power dynamics at play.

"It was more than just a challenge," Albert growled. "That woman was taking away everything I had."

"Do you know why she wanted to go to the rainforest?" Winston asked, eager to shift the focus.

"Didn't ask," Albert responded briskly. "She requested me as her driver and asked to go to the rainforest. Took a little detour, tried to show her some city charm...wouldn't say she really appreciated it though."

"Do you know if anyone else was with her there?"

"Just her," Albert answered. "As far as I knew, it was just going to be her in the rainforest. That was the last I saw."

As Winston walked away, leaving Albert with his rumbling taxi and burdensome thoughts, he pondered how volatile resentment could become if not managed properly — a flame which could engulf the careers and lives of even those most loved. The rain pattered against his umbrella, but beneath it, his mind was turning.

In the daunting terrain of a mountain climbing site, Floyd meets his untimely demise through the barrel of a shotgun, leaving Detective Winston with a chilling whodunit mystery on his hands with prime suspects being Francis and Camille.

As Winston was driving to the mountain climbing site, he went over his notes on Camille. Camille, Floyd's daughter, seemed like the kind of young rich heiress that didn't need much but still desired more. She'd been seen shopping extravagantly and her credit card statements were full of high-ticket items, including a purchase from a local gun shop just a few days before Floyd's demise. 

On reaching the crime scene, he noticed a shotgun lying nearby. Was this the weapon used to kill Floyd? His experiences from the past suggested that you should never jump to conclusions.

In Winston's notes, it was mentioned that Camille was often spotted at the local shooting range, practicing with a shotgun during the summer. Camille had undertaken shooting classes the previous summer. She even held a valid shotgun permit. 

On his return to the office, Winston stopped by Camille's residence. She had large, empty display cases, which seemed odd for a girl who spends so much. Winston speculated about what she might be collecting.

Seeing his puzzled look, Camille casually mentioned, "I've always loved animals."

Despite her lavish spending habits, she's surprisingly not involved in crafts that require stuffing materials. She confirmed this when Winston inquired about it. Although, she was once spotted at a local craft store checkout line with bags of stuffing materials.

When Winston asked her about this, she said, "Oh, that wasn't for me. I was picking it up for a friend."

"It's a healthy hobby," said Camille when asked about her shotgun permit, while showing him the piece of identification. 

Winston was also informed of Floyd's plans to change his will by his attorney. Camille found the updated will in Floyd's study. She didn't seem perturbed by the changes. 

Before he could delve deeper, his phone rang. It was his lieutenant notifying him about a mysterious loan taken by Camille. "Interesting," thought Winston, as he adopted his signature poker face.

As Winston left Camille's property, he had more questions than answers. Camille's story had many sides and each was a step in a journey full of riddles. Winston knew he needed to investigate further. His virus scanner, gut instinct, was telling him this case was stranger than he thought.

Winston perused the local newspaper, his eyes momentarily pausing on an article announcing a lottery winner named Floyd. It was not the lottery part that grabbed his attention but a picture of Floyd on one of his many solo mountain climbs. He was known to love these solitary treks, stating often to those who asked that they offered him a much respected sense of tranquility. This time though, he had plans for another solitary mountain climb, despite a streak of lousy weather. "Guess he's celebrating," Winston mumbled to himself, seeing his long-time acquaintance's choice of celebration wasn't much of a surprise. 

He switched off his desk lamp, grabbed his hat, and left to interview his first pertinent individual: a local potter named Francis. Francis had also seen the news about Floyd's lottery win, although the celebration was bittersweet knowing his own financial strain.

Arriving at the location, Winston found Francis gently molding some clay on a wheel. "Francis?" he inquired.

Francis, a tall lanky figure, turned while still working with the pot. "That's me, detective."

"Busy doing some pottery?"

"Yes," the potter replied in a serious tone. "It's my bread and butter. Although, it hasn't been doing well lately. With declining sales, I couldn't even return that loan I took from a shark to keep the business afloat."

Winston continued probing, "Heard you were invited by Floyd on his mountain climbing trip."

Francis washed his hands and turned off the wheel, looking somewhat surprised. "Yes, that's right. But he said he wanted to go alone this time...said he needed the tranquillity. Floyd always prefered to climb alone."

"Interesting..." Winston responded under his breath. "So, you didn't go with Floyd?"

"Nah, I was going to go on a hunting trip of my own instead," Francis replied, reaching for his favorite shotgun leaning against a nearby wall. He almost always used shotguns on these trips. 

Detective Winston knew not to flinch at the sight of the weapon. "Oh, so, you do a lot of hunting, then."

Francis shrugged, laying the shotgun back against the wall. "Yeah, it's a hobby. And a chance to breathe fresh air; not much of it in here, you see."

Winston nodded, taking mental note of the situation. "Well, then, I suppose I'd best let you get back to it. We'll be in touch, Francis."

On his drive back to the precinct, Winston received a call about Francis taking a hefty loan from a shark to revive his sagging pottery business. Winston sighed, took off his hat, and mussed his hair. He knew Floyd, despite his undeniable love for his solitary mountain climbs, was blissfully unaware of Francis' financial situation. It was all just another lead unraveling in this ever-complicated mountain murder.

Target case file:

In a chilling turn of events, Rose is found lifeless in a car, killed by a vial of acid, leading Detective Winston to the affluent suspects, Daisy and Dexter.

Winston was going over the facts of the case when he decided to visit the suspect, Daisy. Daisy wasn't your typical suspect - she was a singer who always had a passion for her art form, a passion that stood in sharp contrast with her family's dismissive attitude.

“I'm just trying to get ahead in life, you know?" she told Winston as they sat in a small cafe near one of her repeat performance venues - an old building that was frequently harshly criticised for its lack of cleanliness. "They never cared about my music… always thought it was just a phase. I couldn't stand their lack of support.”

Getting rid of her family members from her contacts was, as she put it, a "cleansing experience". It was all very telling of Daisy's meticulous nature - she extended the same cleanliness philosophy to everything in her personal life, hygiene being her top priority; it gave a stark contrast to the venues in which she performed.

After a moment of silence, she casually added, "Sometimes my sarcasm gets the best of me. I can't tell you how many family dinners I've ruined with it. My sarcasm stings so hard, it often leaves them in tears."

Winston thought about Rose, who often parked her car in the same vicinity. "You were scheduled to perform at a place near that parking lot that day… right?" he asked. Daisy affirmed the fact and mentioned having seen Rose's car, acknowledging that she and Rose were the last two people in the vehicle after her show that night.

As part of her performances, Daisy often integrated different kinds of acid into her routines - the same kind, as it turned out, that had been used to murder Rose. A cold chill ran down Winston’s spine as he mentally cross-checked the evidence list.

“Acid isn’t a typical instrument for a singer, Daisy..." Winston quizzed, trying to keep the conversation casual. Daisy just shrugged, "Got to create a spectacle, right? Attract an audience?”

Daisy had always been adamant about not attending any family gatherings - a fact that did not change even after Rose’s death. But she claimed to hold no ill-will towards Rose. As Winston got up from the table to leave, he turned one final time to look at Daisy who was now alone and engrossed in her phone. A suspect or not, one thing was certain, the story was far from over.

Winston reeked of grease and sweat as he strolled into the electronics store, blinking against the twisted glare of neon and the sharp gleam of fluorescent lights. Dexter, a wiry man in neatly pressed slacks and a polo, paused in checking and restocking the freshly stocked batteries to greet him.

"You look lost, sir," he called, a spark in his eyes belying the monotony in his voice.

"Actually, I have a few questions for you, if that's not too much trouble," Winston started, flipping open his notepad to gather his thoughts.

A flicker of unease crossed Dexter’s face, but he masked it quickly, "Sure, always happy to help."

Winston dove straight in, "Know a woman by the name of Rose?"

Dexter's face tightened imperceptibly. "Rose, yeah. I know of her. She left her car here to get cleaned the other day. She told me that she had found an embarrassing picture of me somewhere."

"So, you work on cars too?"

"I... not exactly. I was on duty when she came by. We don't usually offer those services, but I took care of it," he replied, his gaze straying to the poster advertising their recently received new stock of batteries.

"What type of cleaning, exactly?" Winston asked, silently noting another stain on the pristine floors.

"Uh... just vacuuming, mostly. People leave all kinds of things in their cars," he concluded, avoiding Winston's steely gaze. "I found the embarrassing photo of myself in there, the one she had claimed to have found earlier."

"Must have seen a lot of interesting things."

"Yeah, you could say that." Dexter's voice wavered, a hint of bitterness creeping in.

"Were you alone while cleaning the car?"

"Yes. What's this about?" Panic fluttered in Dexter's eyes just as Winston showed him the same embarrassing photo of Dexter that was making the rounds in town - the one Rose had found.

"Oh," Dexter spoke, all hints of his usual smug demeanor nowhere in sight. "That... was circulating at the town gathering... and Rose had grabbed it and laughed at me as she shown it all around."

"Right," Winston said, making a mental note as he slipped the photo back into the folder. The laughter, Rose's cruel laughter at Dexter during that town gathering, rang in his memory. 

Dexter spoke after a pause, "I...didn't know she still had that."

"One more question," Winston started, leaving the silence to hang as Dexter looked about to collapse. "Your education...you studied Chemistry? Specialization, was it industrial acids?"

"Different types, yes," Dexter confirmed, struggling to keep composure. "Hydrochloric, Sulfuric, Nitric...so many..." His voice trailed off into a whisper as Winston closed his notepad.

"Interesting," Winston remarked, and headed for the door. The fluorescent store lights flickered as he strode out into the evening, leaving a bewildered Dexter behind in the now-quiet electronics store.
